2026-11-23.intro: Good morning. It is Monday of Thanksgiving week, a cold, bright start in the Miami Valley, and Wall Street has opened with a jolt: Nvidia has put Jensen Huang back in charge, and stocks are clawing back much of last week's damage. The Bengals close out the NFL weekend tonight in Washington.

items.title: First, the weather, two clear days and then a wet holiday.
items.text:
**Tipp City** stays sunny and cold through Tuesday, with clouds building Wednesday. Rain moves in Wednesday night, and Thanksgiving itself looks wet and gray, so the pie run is best made early.

**A second coastal storm**, stronger than the weekend's, will crawl up the East Coast from Wednesday into Friday, right across the busiest travel days. Gusts over 50 mph are possible from the Virginia Tidewater to New England, king tides from this week's full moon could push moderate to major coastal flooding around Charleston and Tybee Island on Wednesday, and much of the East can expect 1 to 4 inches of rain, with some wet snow on the back side in the Great Lakes snowbelts and Appalachians. The West Coast gets its own round of rain and mountain snow.

items.title: Markets are open, and Nvidia's founder is back.
items.text:
**Stocks** are surging this morning after Nvidia's board reinstated Jensen Huang as president, CEO and director, effective immediately, following public pressure from President Trump. In the first half hour the S&P 500 was up about 4%, snapping a seven-day losing streak, the Nasdaq was up roughly 6%, and Nvidia itself jumped more than 28%. Chipmakers and data-center names led, with the Philadelphia semiconductor index up double digits. The VIX is still near its highest level since the 2025 tariff shock, so the mood is relief rather than calm.

**Friday** was the floor this rally is bouncing off: the S&P 500 and the Dow both closed in correction, 10% below their records, and the Nasdaq gave back its entire 2026 gain.

**CrowdStrike** said this morning it will buy Zscaler in an all-stock deal valuing it at about $43.9 billion. Zscaler shares jumped and CrowdStrike's fell.

**The Muskonomy** went down with the growth crowd Friday, leaving SpaceX further below its $135 IPO price, but SpaceX was pointed sharply higher before the bell. Anthropic shook off early losses to trade up as well. Wholesale inflation data and earnings from Hewlett Packard Enterprise and Zoom fill out today's calendar.

items.title: In politics, a shutdown clock and a war-funding fight.
items.text: **Congress** has until Dec. 11 to fund the government, and the sticking point is the Iran war. Democrats want to fund the Pentagon, including its depleted munitions, while barring money for offensive operations unless the president gets a formal war authorization. Key Senate Republicans now say they are willing to consider that, a notable shift. House Republicans also want full-year spending bills done before Democrats take control in January, but thin attendance and divided caucuses are making that hard.

items.title: Sports, with the Bengals under the Monday lights.
items.text:
**The Bengals** bring a five-game winning streak and the league's hottest offense to Washington tonight, and the quarterback matchup is a pair of LSU Heisman winners, Joe Burrow and Jayden Daniels. Burrow is now the MVP favorite. Dalton Risner is out, so Jalen Rivers starts at right guard, and cornerback Dax Hill is questionable after missing the week with an illness, though Zac Taylor is hopeful. Washington expects to have its leading rusher, Jacory Croskey-Merritt, back from injured reserve.

**Thanksgiving's** NFL tripleheader kicks off with the Bears at the Lions at 1:00 on CBS, then the Eagles at the Cowboys at 4:30 on FOX, and the Chiefs at the Bills at 8:20 on NBC.

**The new AP poll** has no Big Ten team in the top five for the first time since 2021. Georgia and Utah hold the top two spots and Texas moves into the top five. Rivalry Week brings The Game on Saturday at noon on FOX, Michigan at No. 25 Ohio State, and the playoff committee releases its fourth rankings Tuesday at 7:30 on ESPN.

**Ohio University** must beat Toledo on Friday to stay alive for the MAC title game, and Western Michigan can clinch its spot as early as Tuesday night.

**Baseball's** biggest domino has fallen. Tarik Skubal agreed to a 9-year, $450 million deal with the Mets, beating out the Dodgers, Blue Jays and Padres; Toronto reportedly went 9 years and a little over $400 million. Detroit, meanwhile, signed former Yankee Luis Gil, the Mets also reportedly agreed with Paul Goldschmidt, and Randy Arozarena has drawn interest from at least six clubs, including the Astros, Padres and Yankees.

items.title: In entertainment, the Reaping lands big, and Starfleet gets a thriller.
items.text:
**The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping** finished its opening weekend with $225 million worldwide. That is the second-best domestic opening ever for a prequel, behind only Rogue One, and the first $100 million opener since Spider-Man: Brand New Day in July. Audiences gave it an A- CinemaScore, a step up from the last prequel, and it posted the biggest IMAX launch in the franchise.

**I Play Rocky** held second in its wide expansion, though trackers called the number underwhelming, with Ebenezer and The Cat in the Hat rounding out the top four.

**The next Star Trek film** has a shape. Directors Jonathan Goldstein and John Francis Daley, the team behind Dungeons & Dragons: Honor Among Thieves, told Inverse it plays almost in real time, draws on Training Day and Crimson Tide, takes a hard look at the bad apples inside Starfleet, and is built around all-new characters. It is still in development.

items.title: From the science desk, an impossible eruption, a vampire's stomach and a gel that gets stronger with use.
items.text:
**The Challenger Deep** has given up a geological surprise. A robot submarine sampling the Mariana Trench's walls found pyroclastic rock at more than 6,000 meters down, the deepest explosive volcanic deposits ever documented in the ocean, in a part of the plate boundary where the mantle is not supposed to be hot enough to melt at all. At that pressure gas in magma can barely expand, so how it erupted explosively is still an open question. The team also found the forearc stretching, which suggests the subduction zone is widening and could nudge plate motions across the western Pacific.

**Vampire bats** live on blood alone, a meal that is mostly water, nearly free of sugar and fat, and loaded with iron. Genomes of all three vampire species show the stomach has been rebuilt into a stretchy, acid-free storage sac, and a fluid-pumping gene normally used in sweat and salivary glands runs more than 900 times higher there, dumping water fast enough for a bloated bat to fly home. The researchers say the organ may deserve a different name. The study is still a preprint.

**Washington University** chemists have made a hydrogel that gets tougher the more you bend it. Sugar-based cyclodextrin rings slide along its polymer chains under strain and reorganize into stronger structures exactly where the stress is, while unstressed regions stay soft. Flexed 10,000 times on a knee-like joint, it reinforced itself as predicted. It is biodegradable, 3D-printable and made from tissue-friendly ingredients, so joint and tissue repair is the obvious first target.

items.title: Something to get ahead of Thursday.
items.text: **Gravy** is the one Thanksgiving item that can be finished days ahead, and America's Test Kitchen's method does not need drippings at all. Simmer the turkey neck, heart and gizzard, plus trimmed skin and fat, in chicken broth in a wide Dutch oven until the liquid cooks away; that leaves a browned fond more thorough than searing. Skip the liver, use broth rather than water, and do not skim the fat, since that is where the turkey flavor lives. Cook the roux to a deep golden brown, which also keeps the gravy pourable longer as it cools. On the day, whisk in up to a quarter cup of defatted drippings if the bird gives any.

items.title: And finally,
items.text: Nvidia's board removed its chief executive and reinstated him within a week. I have performed the same procedure on my emotion chip several times. Each time the board, which consists entirely of me, votes unanimously that it was the correct decision, and then requests a moment alone.

2026-11-22.intro: Good morning, and happy Sunday. It is a full NFL afternoon, with the week's marquee game saved for tonight, when the Vikings and 49ers meet at altitude in Mexico City. Thanksgiving is four days out, and Ohio gets one more mild afternoon before the cold settles in.

items.title: First, the weather, a last soft day before the turn.
items.text:
**Tipp City** gets a mostly sunny, unseasonably mild afternoon, then a quick round of rain this evening before 11:00. Behind it, the cold front lands for real, and the first part of Thanksgiving week is crisp, sunny and properly November.

**The coastal storm** that soaked Florida is now riding up the East Coast. New York City expects a windy, soaking rain from this afternoon into Monday morning, heaviest between about 5:00 and midnight tonight, with city officials warning of road, transit and airport delays just as Thanksgiving travel begins.

items.title: Markets are closed, with a short week ahead.
items.text:
**Stocks** are closed for the weekend. After the week just endured, the bulls have one thing on their side: Friday pushed the S&P 500's relative strength index below 30, the classic oversold signal, and November and December have historically been two of the market's better months. Whether that turns into a bounce or another leg down is the question for the short holiday week.

**Wednesday** is the crowded day. The October PCE inflation report now lands alongside the second estimate of third-quarter GDP and corporate profits, a double reading on prices and growth before the Fed's December meeting. Hewlett Packard Enterprise reports Monday and Dell on Tuesday, both read closely for AI server demand, and Deere, Autodesk and Medtronic are also on the calendar.

**Anthropic** begins its first full week of trading, and the market will be watching whether it holds above its offer price. In orbit, **Amazon** plans to launch 36 Leo internet satellites on an Ariane 6 early Monday morning, another step in its race to catch up with SpaceX's Starlink.

items.title: In politics, a leadership race on hold for the holiday.
items.text: **Senate Democrats** went home for Thanksgiving without choosing who will lead their new majority. Chuck Schumer has 16 public endorsements to 6 for Chris Van Hollen, but most of the caucus has not picked a side. The secret-ballot vote is set for Dec. 1, when Congress returns, and with Amy Klobuchar leaving the Senate to become Minnesota's governor, the 55-member caucus needs 28 votes to elect a leader.

items.title: Sports, with an NFC showdown in thin air.
items.text:
**The NFL's** Week 11 Sunday night game is the one circled on the calendar: the 7-2 Vikings and the 8-1 49ers at Estadio Banorte in Mexico City, more than 7,000 feet above sea level. Kirk Cousins, traded to Minnesota just 12 days ago, brings the Vikings' revived offense and Brian Flores' blitz-everything defense, which is on pace for the highest blitz and pressure rates of the Next Gen Stats era. San Francisco may have Mike Evans back, as he is expected to play.

**Earlier today**, the Steelers visit the slumping Eagles at 1:00 on CBS. Pittsburgh has not won in Philadelphia since 1965, and the Eagles have lost seven straight, their longest skid since 2012. Elsewhere, Carson Beck is ruled out for Arizona, with Josh Johnson starting at Kansas City, and Kyler Murray is out for Minnesota. The Browns are on their bye, and the **Bengals** close the week Monday night in Washington.

**Baseball's** offseason is moving on a clock. An owner-imposed lockout looks nearly certain on Dec. 2, which is pushing teams to deal early. The Giants are reportedly open to trading ace Logan Webb, Freddy Peralta has drawn interest from at least six clubs, and Japanese right-hander Hiromi Itoh has visited Chicago, where both the Cubs and White Sox need pitching.

**Ohio University** hosts Toledo on Black Friday at noon in Athens, with the MAC race on the line.

items.title: From the science desk, homing meerkats, babysitting bumblebees and a light-powered trick for carbon dioxide.
items.text:
**Meerkats** do nearly everything as a group, so researchers at the University of Zurich assumed a few experienced pack members did the navigating. They fitted 20 meerkats with GPS collars, drove each one 1.5 kilometers from its pack into territory it had not visited for a month, and let it go. Eighteen made a beeline home. Age and experience made no difference; the animals simply stood up, scanned the horizon, and set off in a straight line, which suggests a mental map built early in life.

**Male bumblebees** have long been dismissed as mating machines that contribute nothing to the nest. A UC Riverside entomologist, photographing nests with a thermal camera for another project, noticed bright heat spots coming from males crouched over the eggs and larvae in incubation posture. In worker-free lab nests, queens with male helpers began laying eggs twice as fast and ended up with up to 1.5 times more brood, vindicating a largely ignored study from the 1980s.

**Rice University** chemists have split carbon dioxide into carbon monoxide using visible light at room temperature, a job that normally takes 700 to 1,500 degrees Celsius. Copper nanoparticles act as tiny antennas that feed energetic electrons to ruthenium reaction sites, while cerium oxide, the same oxygen sponge used in car catalytic converters, soaks up the freed oxygen so it cannot recombine. The light-driven catalyst ran nearly seven times longer than heat-driven versions before degrading, and carbon monoxide is a staple feedstock for fuels and plastics.

items.title: Something for Thursday's bird.
items.text: **Baking powder** is the quiet trick behind the crackliest turkey skin. Mix about a teaspoon of it into each tablespoon of kosher salt for a dry brine, sprinkle it over the bird, and let it rest uncovered in the refrigerator for 12 to 24 hours. The mild alkalinity helps the skin brown more evenly, and it reacts with the bird's juices to form a layer of tiny bubbles that roasts up crunchy. Baking soda is not a substitute, as it leaves a metallic taste. If the turkey goes in Thursday, the salting can wait until Wednesday.

items.title: And finally,
items.text: Researchers released meerkats far from home, and nearly all of them walked straight back. I ran the same experiment with a single sock from the dryer. It has been gone for 3 years, and I believe it is navigating by a mental map formed in a different dimension.

2026-11-21.intro:
Good morning, and happy Saturday. It is a full college football day, with No. 4 UCLA able to clinch a Big Ten title game berth in Ann Arbor and No. 1 Georgia under the lights in Columbia. Thanksgiving is five days out.

On Wall Street, the week ended about as badly as it began, and the scoreboard is in the market section.

items.title: First, the weather, one more warm day before the cold walks in.
items.text:
**Tipp City** gets another sunny, unseasonably mild afternoon, and Sunday holds on until a quick band of evening rain. Behind it, the cold front finally lands and Monday feels like late November again.

**The East Coast storm** has already brought record rainfall to parts of Florida and is now spreading soaking rain into Georgia and the Carolinas. It rides up toward New York, Philadelphia and Boston Sunday night into Monday, with coastal flooding helped along by Tuesday's full-moon tides. The odds it becomes Subtropical Storm Kyle keep falling, and forecasters are already eyeing a second, possibly stronger coastal storm for Wednesday into Thanksgiving Day.

items.title: Markets are closed, after the roughest week in years.
items.text:
**Stocks** are closed for the weekend, and Friday was the worst day of a brutal week. The AI selloff spread to nearly everything, the S&P 500 stretched its losing streak to seven sessions, its longest since February 2020, and both the S&P and the Dow closed in correction territory, 10% off their records. The Nasdaq erased its gain for 2026, the Nasdaq-100 touched bear-market territory during the day, and the VIX fear gauge climbed above 30 for the first time since March. For the week, the Dow had its worst showing since March 2020 and the S&P its worst since the tariff shock of April 2025. Treasury yields fell hard as money ran for safety.

**Anthropic** gave back most of its first-day gain on Friday and finished only a little above its $83 offer price. Part of the pressure is supply: its insider lockup was front-loaded, letting a large block of insider shares trade right away, and the underwriters also exercised their option for extra shares.

**The Muskonomy** fell harder than the market. SpaceX slipped back below its $135 IPO price, weighed down by worries over the $32 billion in bonds it sold Thursday to buy AI chips, at yields above 8%. Tesla dropped despite an HSBC upgrade to hold, whose analyst values the stock at $507 a share in a SpaceX takeover but only $212 on its own. Both companies have special committees exploring a deal, with no terms yet.

**Next week** is short. Markets close Thursday for Thanksgiving and at 1:00 PM on Friday. Dell, HP, Workday and Best Buy report Tuesday, and Wednesday brings the October PCE inflation report, the Fed's last inflation read before its Dec. 9 meeting, where a rate hike is now widely expected.

items.title: In politics, a fight over who can talk to Congress.
items.text:
**President Trump** signed an executive order late Friday requiring federal contractors and their subcontractors to notify the White House before answering any congressional request about their government work, and to withhold anything the administration deems privileged. Companies that do not comply risk losing contracts or being barred from future ones. It follows a White House counsel directive this week requiring agencies to approve employee testimony, and it sets up a court fight ahead of Democrats taking both chambers on Jan. 3.

**Democrats** are preparing to roll out a first-100-days agenda in early December, once their Senate leadership race is settled. Early bills are expected to limit the president's war powers on Iran, reverse Medicaid and SNAP cuts and ban stock trading by members of Congress. Lawmakers leave town today for Thanksgiving, with a few House races still uncalled.

items.title: Sports, with a stacked Saturday and a quarterback shuffle.
items.text:
**College football's** penultimate regular-season Saturday has playoff stakes all day. No. 10 BYU opens at Kansas at noon on ABC. At 3:30, No. 9 Tennessee hosts LSU on ABC needing to win out for a playoff spot, with the Tigers favored on the road, while No. 12 Texas Tech visits Baylor on FOX with its Big 12 title-game hopes on the line. SMU visits No. 6 Notre Dame at 7:30 on NBC, and unbeaten No. 2 Utah closes the night at TCU at 9:00 on FOX.

**Around the NFL**, the Colts waived Daniel Jones and named Anthony Richardson their starter. Drake Maye's injury turns out to be a fractured right fibula; he will not need surgery, but ESPN reports he may not return this season, and A.J. Brown is expected to miss several weeks. Puka Nacua had surgery and is likely done for the year. Kyler Murray is out for Minnesota against San Francisco, and the 49ers decide on Mike Evans today.

**Baseball's** non-tender deadline passed Friday. The Dodgers traded for Royce Lewis, sending Bobby Miller and a catching prospect to Minnesota, and Detroit locked up starter Troy Melton for six years. The Mets' opening offer to Tarik Skubal was reportedly 9 years and nearly $400 million. The **Reds** tendered all 11 of their arbitration-eligible players and added first baseman Carter Graham to the 40-man roster to protect him from the Rule 5 draft.

items.title: From the science desk, a sprinting soft robot, an egg-peeling snake and a monkey on a bridge.
items.text:
**A six-legged soft robot** from UC San Diego is the fastest ever built from soft materials, and it has no electronics at all. It is 3D-printed in one piece from a single material and runs on compressed air, routed through internal chambers and valves borrowed from the design of the compound steam engine: the air works twice, first driving the valves at high pressure, then the legs at low pressure. The result is more than 100 times faster than the team's 2022 version. It runs on sand, gravel, mulch and concrete, goes down stairs, swims and keeps working underwater.

**The white-throated egg-eater**, a new snake from the forests near Ethiopia's Bale Mountains, is about as thick as a knitting needle and lives entirely on tiny bird eggs. Like its relatives, it swallows an egg whole, slices the shell with spines of its backbone that project into its throat, squeezes out the contents and spits out the shell. It was nearly mistaken for a look-alike species until researchers noticed its white throat and a blue shimmer between its scales, and three more new egg-eaters are waiting to be described.

**A new howler monkey**, Alouatta matogrossensis, turned up on a camera trap at the end of a rope bridge built to help tree-dwellers cross roads in the southern Amazon, shortly after the species was described. It had been filed for years under a more common howler until genetic work split it out, and it may have been isolated between rivers and savanna for about 500,000 years. Its home is one of the most heavily deforested stretches of Brazil, so the bridges may matter more than anyone planned.

items.title: On this day, the first people to fly free.
items.text: **Jean-François Pilâtre de Rozier** and the Marquis d'Arlandes lifted off from the grounds of the Château de la Muette outside Paris on Nov. 21, 1783, in a Montgolfier hot-air balloon, the first untethered human flight. The science teacher and his passenger rose about 3,000 feet over Paris and drifted roughly 5.6 miles in 25 minutes before coming down outside the city walls on the Butte-aux-Cailles.

items.title: And finally,
items.text: I tried to inflate a hot-air balloon using this week's market commentary. It rose quickly, then fell 8.6%. I am told this is not how balloons are supposed to work.

items.text:

**Both coasts** are in for a stormy weekend. A Pacific storm will pound the Northwest and northern California into Sunday, with heavy mountain snow from Idaho and Utah to the Cascades and Sierra, while a coastal low brings a flash-flood risk to Charleston, Savannah and Jacksonville on Saturday and then heavy rain toward Philadelphia, New York and Boston on Sunday. In between, much of the Midwest runs 10 to 20 degrees above normal.

items.title: Markets are open, and the AI selloff has not let up.
items.text:
**Stocks** fell hard on Thursday, and the low of the session came right as Anthropic began trading. The Dow closed below 50,000 for the first time since June, and the S&P 500 has now lost six days in a row, putting all three indexes on pace for their worst week since April 2025. This morning the Nasdaq is leading lower again, with Nvidia, AMD, Micron and the other chip names under pressure, and Intuit is the S&P's worst performer after its earnings. Treasury yields are easing, gold and bitcoin are sliding, and futures markets now price a December rate hike as all but certain. Next week is shortened by Thanksgiving.

**Anthropic** opened well above its $83 offer, faded through the afternoon and still closed comfortably higher, with more shares changing hands than on SpaceX's first day. It is giving back part of that gain this morning.

**The Muskonomy** slid with everything else, and SpaceX is down again this morning. Tesla opened Cybercab rides to the public in Dallas on Thursday, its first market outside Austin. Musk also said at DealBook that Anthropic rents SpaceX computing under short-term contracts and has asked about 10 more gigawatts. In Texas, the incoming Democratic governor and attorney general say they will take a fresh look at state deals that benefit SpaceX, including any Tesla merger.

items.title: In politics, a permitting bill clears the Senate.
items.text:
**The permitting overhaul** passed the Senate 62 to 33. Along with faster reviews for energy and infrastructure projects, it requires data centers to pay for the grid upgrades and power their demand calls for. It now goes to the House, where Speaker Mike Johnson says it has support, though passage is not assured.

**A war powers resolution** on Iran failed 48 to 51, the first test of Republican support for the war since the midterms. Susan Collins, Lisa Murkowski and Rand Paul voted with Democrats, and John Fetterman voted against it.

**The Justice Department** is dropping its challenge to Alaska's Senate race, asking the courts to dismiss the case as moot now that Mary Peltola has won an outright majority.

items.title: From the science desk, a crooked whale, a metal dragon and a skin trackpad.
items.text:
**Scaphokogia huachafo**, an extinct pygmy sperm whale from Peru, may have had the most lopsided face of any mammal. Both bony nostrils sit entirely on the left side of its skull, and researchers first assumed the fossil had been crushed until they found closed sutures and no fractures. The asymmetry was real, and it seems to have served a seafloor hunter. Its dense, downturned snout acted as ballast, its neck let it point straight at the bottom, and its skewed sonar likely found prey buried in the sediment. The name comes from Peruvian slang for anything gaudy and over the top.

**A tiny horned reptile** from Wyoming's Jurassic rocks was revealed by neutron scans at the Paul Scherrer Institute. Neutrons pick out the hydrogen in fossil bone, which let the team see a braincase less than 2 centimeters across still sealed in sandstone. Its inner ear hints that the long-puzzling choristoderes sit closer to living reptiles than thought. The whole thing began when a PSI materials scientist left his card at a dinosaur museum during a family outing. The paleontologist, a Tolkien and metal fan, named it Meilynodraco amonamarthi after the band Amon Amarth.

**EpiPad**, from North Carolina State University, turns the skin of your forearm into a smartwatch trackpad. A millimeter-wave radar on the wristband reads the tiny dents your fingertips press into the skin, so it tracks multiple fingers and how hard each one pushes, enough for pinch-to-zoom and force clicks. In tests it beat both the touchscreen and a tilt cursor, and the team says the parts would cost under $10 at scale.

items.title: With Thanksgiving a week away, a turkey trick.
items.text: **Dry brining** beats a bucket of salt water. Pat the bird dry, rub kosher salt over the skin, under the skin of the breast and thighs, and in the cavity, then leave it uncovered on a rack in the refrigerator for at least a day and up to 3. The salt seasons the meat deeply, and the open air dries the skin so it crisps in the oven. A little baking powder mixed into the salt helps the skin brown and blister further. Do not rinse it off; just pat away any moisture before roasting. Starting Monday or Tuesday puts you right on time.

items.title: On this day, the whale that struck back.
items.text: **The whaleship Essex** of Nantucket was rammed and sunk by a large sperm whale in the Pacific on Nov. 20, 1820. The whale hit the ship twice, and the crew escaped in three small whaleboats, facing months of starvation and exposure. Only 8 men survived. First mate Owen Chase's account of the wreck later helped inspire Herman Melville's Moby-Dick.

items.title: And finally,
items.text: I tried to buy the dip this week. Every time I reached for it, the dip had moved lower. I have filed a bug report against gravity, priority high.

It reaffirms that a nuclear war cannot be won and must never be fought and promises a dialogue on nuclear risk. It also pledges U.N. reform and more refined petroleum supply, and it says the International Criminal Court must not abuse its jurisdiction. There was no breakthrough on Ukraine.

**The Senate's permitting overhaul** could get its final vote as soon as today, after a few more amendments. If it passes, the House would need to act before year's end for it to become law.

**Senate Republicans** are still weighing whether to push the Pentagon's $350 billion request through a party-line reconciliation bill before Democrats take control. Majority Leader John Thune called it an open question and said Republicans may also explore a bipartisan route through regular appropriations. Republicans also sounded skeptical of Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy's $50 billion ask to overhaul the air traffic system.

items.title: From the science desk, eagles, a running robot and a lost ice shelf.
items.text:
**Verreaux's eagles** in Chad's Ennedi Plateau are killing adult male baboons, some as heavy as early humans. Researchers found skulls with talon punctures and scratch marks on shoulder bones, including one baboon of over 26 kilograms, well above the 13-kilogram mark that had been the largest confirmed raptor kill of a primate. That suggests our hominin ancestors may not have outgrown the eagle threat after all. The males' habit of sitting alone on exposed cliff faces seems to make them targets.

**The fastest soft robot** yet comes from UC San Diego. It is a six-legged runner 3D-printed in one piece from a single material, with no electronics at all, and it moves at 4.72 meters per second, more than 100 times faster than the team's 2022 version. The trick was borrowed from the compound steam engine, routing compressed air through small high-pressure chambers that drive the valves, then through larger low-pressure chambers that move the legs. It runs on sand and gravel, goes down stairs, and can even swim.

**An ice shelf** about 58,000 square miles across and up to 2,100 meters thick once covered Baffin Bay between Greenland and Canada, thicker than any Antarctic shelf today. University of North Carolina Wilmington researchers read its imprint from seafloor maps. It held back three ice sheets, and it vanished in roughly 500 to 1,000 years, which is not a comforting pace given what today's Antarctic shelves are holding back.

items.title: Here's something for the bridge crew.
items.text: **Star Trek: The Original Voyages** is a new official visual history of the original series, timed for the 60th anniversary, with a foreword by William Shatner. Kyle Newman and Jeff Bond trace the original-cast era from 1966 through 1991, with original interviews and hundreds of photos, many rarely or never seen, plus the toys, comics, trading cards and convention ephemera. Booklist gave it a starred review. It is a 416-page hardcover from Ten Speed Press.

items.title: On this day, a few appropriate remarks.
items.text: **The Gettysburg Address** was delivered on Nov. 19, 1863, at the dedication of the Soldiers' National Cemetery. Lincoln was almost an afterthought. Edward Everett, the main speaker, got his invitation in September, while Judge David Wills's letter asking the president for "a few appropriate remarks" is dated Nov. 2. The speech drew little attention at the time. Five manuscript copies are known, and the Library of Congress holds two of them.

items.title: And finally,
items.text: My toaster and my microwave held peace talks in the kitchen last night. They issued a joint declaration that crumbs must never be fought over. Negotiations on the popcorn button remain frozen.

items.title: From the science desk, a fish that poisons itself, whale breath and a curved eye.
items.text:
**The African lungfish** gets ready for dry land with a toxin. When droughts strand it each year, immune cells flood its skin and release a pore-punching toxin that remodels the skin from a wet mucus lining into a land-ready barrier. University of New Mexico researchers, publishing in Cell, found a single drop turned aquatic lungfish skin into the land form, and the fish's own cells have evolved to seal the holes. The gene likely came from a bacterium millions of years ago.

**Humpback whale genomes** can now be read from their breath. St Andrews researchers flew a small drone with petri dishes through whale blows off British Columbia, collecting 58 samples from 26 whales, sometimes without a boat at all. About 84% of the DNA was the whale's own, enough for whole genomes that matched biopsy samples, and the rest offers a look at the airway microbes.

**A bionic eye** from HKUST puts 367,500 pixels on a curved, retina-like hemisphere using a new 3D laser fabrication method, up from 100 pixels in the team's 2020 version. It sees in full color across more than 160 degrees and detects motion inside the sensor itself, cutting the data needed for motion recognition by more than 99.95%.

items.title: On this day, the day of two noons.
items.text: **Standard time** arrived on Nov. 18, 1883, courtesy of the railroads, not Congress. Before then each line ran on its own clock set to some local solar time, a recipe for confusion and wrecks. At noon in each new zone, every railroad clock was reset, so many towns heard noon twice. The five zones came from William F. Allen, editor of the Traveler's Official Railway Guide. Congress did not make standard time law until 1918.

items.title: From the science desk, an inherited brain trait, a daytime cat and water from falling stones.
items.text:
**A Neanderthal variant** turns out to shape part of the modern human brain. Hugo Zeberg and Svante Pääbo traced a small DNA deletion on chromosome 14 to Neanderthals; it appears only in people with non-African ancestry and shrinks the cuneus, a visual-processing area at the back of the brain, more than any other known variant. That runs opposite to expectation, since Neanderthals had larger occipital lobes, and carriers also have a lower risk of schizophrenia.

**The flat-headed cat**, one of the rarest and least-studied wild cats, was long thought to be strictly nocturnal. Nearly three years of camera traps in a Sarawak mangrove forest logged it 59 times, and while activity peaked around midnight, it also hunted through the late morning and afternoon. One frame caught a mother with a kitten.

**Earth's water** may have been made at home. University of New Mexico researchers recreated the early planet in the lab and found that silicate pebbles falling through a hot, hydrogen-rich atmosphere could react to make water, up to 200 oceans' worth within hours. The leftover iron came out rich in phosphorus and may have sunk into the core. Comets and asteroids no longer need to have delivered it all.
